title: Master Yinguang on the Conflated Edition of the Amitāyus Sutra
author: Zhiyu
excerpt: In the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, there are three passages that discuss the conflated edition of the Amitāyus Sutra, and these are now widely cited as irrefutable proof that Master Yinguang opposed the conflated edition. In fact, from these three passages one can clearly see that Master Yinguang did not oppose the conflated edition at all, nor did he ever say that the Amitāyus Sutra could not be conflated. He held, rather, that the Amitāyus Sutra can be conflated.

inline.s: In the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, there are three passages that discuss the conflated edition of the Amitāyus Sutra, and these are now widely cited as irrefutable proof that Master Yinguang opposed the conflated edition. In fact, from these three passages one can clearly see:
Master Yinguang did not oppose the conflated edition at all, nor did he ever say that the Amitāyus Sutra could not be conflated.
He held, rather, that the Amitāyus Sutra can be conflated
Let us analyze this as follows.
Master Yinguang said:

“The Amitābha Sutra, the Amitāyus Sutra, and the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life — also called the Sixteen Contemplations Sutra — are known as the Three Pure Land Sutras; with the addition of the Chapter on the Vows of Samantabhadra, they form the Four Pure Land Sutras. Among the printed catalogues there is a copy of the Four Pure Land Sutras, in which the Amitāyus Sutra is the one that Wei Chengguan abridged and, moreover, supplemented from other sutras
(that is, other sutras that are not the Amitāyus Sutra)
to enhance it. Though this may be beneficial in principle, in fact it is a serious error, and it should not be relied upon.”
(from the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Reply to Layman Gao Shaolin, Letter Three)
[Analysis] In this passage, Master Yinguang is saying that Wei Chengguan's conflated edition (referred to as the Wei Conflated Edition) should not
rely on other sutras
(other sutras that are not the original translations of the Amitāyus Sutra)
to supplement it
. This only says that Wei Chengguan's method of conflating was unsuitable,
and it does not say that the Amitāyus Sutra cannot be conflated. For example, Xia Lianju's conflated edition (the Xia Conflated Edition) has no such problem of
supplementing it from other sutras
(other sutras that are not the Amitāyus Sutra)
to enhance it
Master Yinguang said:

“The dissemination of the Buddhadharma is no easy matter. The translation of sutras and treatises is never undertaken lightly; hence in a translation hall there are the chief translator, the interpreter, the verifier of meaning, and the polisher of the wording. How would one dare to transmit and distribute the Buddhist scriptures according to one's own arbitrary discretion.
[Analysis] The above concerns the matter of disseminating the Buddhist scriptures, but a conflated edition is not itself a Buddhist scripture, and so it does not fall within this category.

Wang Longshu's Great Amitāyus Sutra, from the Song dynasty down to the end of the Ming, was practiced by many people. Yet because Master Yunqi [Zhuhong] considered that it still contained unsuitable passages, it gradually fell into obscurity thereafter. Wei Chengguan's learning was not the equal of Longshu's, yet his self-confidence exceeded Longshu's. To work along the traces left by another man makes the task easy; how could Chengguan be said to surpass Longshu? Since Master Lianchi would not even circulate Wang's edition

, how would we dare to circulate Wei's edition and thereby open the door to people's reckless alteration of the Buddhist scriptures? And [it would open the way] for the class of people who denounce Buddhism to say that the Buddhist scriptures were all fabricated by later generations and were not in fact translated from the Buddha's land. Yet this sutra and this treatise, if contemplated by a superior practitioner of true cultivation, are likewise of great benefit.

— for he takes only what is beneficial and is not tainted by its defects. But if an inferior practitioner contemplates them, then before gaining any benefit he first suffers harm, for he only imitates their fault of altering scriptures and censuring the ancients and does not emulate their direct, focused, and single-minded practice. To teach according to the capacity of beings and to prescribe medicine according to the illness — a teaching that does not suit the capacity is the same as a medicine that does not suit the illness. Would I dare, on the strength of one or two acceptable points, to have it widely circulated
(This is to say: one should not circulate the Treatise on the Essence of Amitābha.)
, and thereby leave the inferior practitioner with a fault?”
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Reply to a Certain Layman of Yongjia, Letter Two)
[Analysis]

The above concerns Wang Longshu's conflated edition, the Great Amitāyus Sutra (referred to as the Wang Conflated Edition). Although over the several hundred years from the Song to the end of the Ming many people practiced it, yet because it contained unsuitable passages Master Lianchi no longer circulated it. The Wei Conflated Edition is not even as good as the Wang Conflated Edition, so it too should not be circulated. The Xia Conflated Edition has neither the unsuitable passages that exist in the Wang Conflated Edition nor [those of the others], and is more complete than both the Wang Conflated Edition and the Wei Conflated Edition, so it does not fall within the scope of Master Yinguang's criticism.
Master Yinguang

“How would we dare to circulate Wei's edition and thereby open the door to people's reckless alteration of the Buddhist scriptures, and [give occasion] for the class of people who denounce Buddhism to say that the Buddhist scriptures were all fabricated by later generations and were not in fact translated from the Buddha's land?”

This passage clearly seems to be a criticism directed at someone who circulated the Wei Conflated Edition as though it were a Buddhist scripture (without marking it as a conflated edition). This also sounds a warning for the circulation of conflated editions:
A conflated edition is a conflated edition, not a Buddhist scripture.
When circulating a conflated edition,
one must clearly mark it as a conflated edition
Consider: if a conflated edition were clearly labeled as a conflated edition, how could it

“open the door to people's reckless alteration of the Buddhist scriptures, and [give occasion] for the class of people who denounce Buddhism to say that the Buddhist scriptures were all fabricated by later generations and were not translated from the Buddha's land?”
Because a conflated edition is not at all a Buddhist scripture,
it can hardly be said to be an alteration or a fabrication of the Buddhist scriptures.
The reason Master Lianchi did not circulate the Wang Conflated Edition was not that it was a conflated edition, but that it had
“unsuitable passages.”
Moreover, Master Lianchi,
while regretfully pointing out the unsuitable passages, also praised it, saying:
“Truly, it has rendered great service to the Pure Land!”
Master Lianchi said:
“Layman
(Layman Wang Longshu)
has conflated the four translations
(that is, Layman Wang Longshu conflated the four original translations)
— the words are concise yet the meaning is complete, the phrasing is smooth and the principle is clear.
Truly, it has rendered great service to the Pure Land! It is a pity that
several passages within are not yet settled
it is a pity that
there are several places that are not quite proper)
(from the Daily Recitations of the Various Sutras)
Master Yinguang also did not say that the Amitāyus Sutra could not be conflated; rather, he said that Wei Chengguan conflated it poorly, and that it must not
be circulated as a Buddhist scripture (without being labeled a conflated edition)
Therefore, neither Master Lianchi nor Master Yinguang ever said that the Amitāyus Sutra could not be conflated.
Master Yinguang said:

“In the Amitāyus Sutra there are three grades; in the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life there are nine grades. Those in the three lowest grades are all people who committed evil deeds, yet at the moment of death they encountered a good spiritual friend who instructed them in Buddha-recitation, and so they attained rebirth [in the Pure Land].
Wang Longshu rigidly clung to [the view] that the three grades are precisely the nine grades
(that is, he clung rigidly to the view that the three grades spoken of in the Amitāyus Sutra are the nine grades spoken of in the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life)
; this is the root of the error.

Thus he took the lowest grade [of the three] to be the three lowest grades [of the nine], which is a great error. Hence, in the highest grade he says nothing of the aspiration for bodhi, in the middle grade he speaks of the aspiration for bodhi, and in the lowest grade he says there is no aspiration for bodhi. In the Amitāyus Sutra, all three grades involve the aspiration for bodhi. In the layman Wang's view, the lowest grade [of the three] consists of persons with grave karmic offenses — how could they have the aspiration for bodhi? He did not consider that in the lowest grade [of the three] there is not a single word about committing karmic offenses; rather, these are good people, and they could only be classed as the middle grade among the nine grades. To forcibly make the lowest of the three grades the lowest grade [of the nine], going against the sutra and violating reason, ends up as an arbitrary alteration of the scriptures — and this is a grave offense. In his view, the Buddha was surely gathering in all beings; yet he did not understand that the Buddha gathers only the good kinds of beings and does not reach the evil kinds. Since he took good people to be evil people, he therefore said they had no aspiration for bodhi. Rigidly clinging to [the view] that the lowest of the three grades is the lowest of the nine grades, he mistook good people for evil people. He did not know that among the lowest three of the nine grades, when death is at hand and suffering is extreme, upon once hearing the Buddha's name — the heart that entrusts itself and takes refuge, hoping for the Buddha's compassionate rescue — that heart's courage and gratitude are deeper by ten thousand times than the heart of a convict awaiting pardon at the execution ground. Though it is not spoken of as the aspiration for bodhi, yet the urgency and sincerity of that thought truly fulfill the aspiration for bodhi. It is a pity that Master Wang, not following the meaning of this sutra, relied instead on the Contemplation Sutra and forcibly slandered good people as evil people, in the end judging them as evil. Since even Master Wang had this fault, can later people recklessly pose as great authorities? Since the Amitāyus Sutra already exists, why stir up trouble over nothing? Master Lianchi pointed out Master Wang's error but did not yet explain why he had acted so. Now I will explain the reason for it — it was because he rigidly clung to [the view] that the three grades are the nine grades. I record this, on the one hand to show
the difficulty of conflating [a sutra]
, and on the other hand to forestall the recklessness of later people
(that is, their rigidly clinging to the view that the three grades are the nine grades)
. As for Wei Moshen, there is no need to speak of him; audacious in courage and coarse in heart, he is not a worthy model
(not worth serving as a model to imitate)
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Reply to Layman Wang Zili, Letter Three)
[Analysis] In this passage, Master Yinguang is addressing the problems of the Wang Conflated Edition:
“rigidly clinging to [the view] that the three grades are the nine grades
(that is, rigidly clinging to the view that the three grades spoken of in the Amitāyus Sutra are the nine grades spoken of in the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life)
There is not a single word saying that Wang Longshu should not have conflated [the sutra]. Moreover, at the end Master Yinguang wrote:
“I record this, on the one hand to show
the difficulty of conflating [a sutra]
, and on the other hand to forestall the recklessness of later people
(I write these words above, on the one hand to show
the difficulty of conflating [a sutra]
, and on the other hand to forestall the reckless view of later people who cling rigidly to [the belief] that the three grades are the nine grades)

This is to say: the difficulty of conflating the Amitāyus Sutra is such that a man audacious in courage and coarse in heart like Wei Moshen is not up to the task, and is even less worthy of being a model to imitate.
This also
proves
that Master Yinguang held that the Amitāyus Sutra can be conflated

, but that it must be accomplished by someone capable of it. If Master Yinguang had held that it could not be conflated, he would have said: “I record this, on the one hand to show that it cannot be conflated, and on the other hand to forestall the recklessness of later people.” Rather than saying:
“to show
the difficulty of conflating [a sutra]
In summary, Master Yinguang is saying: one must not circulate a conflated edition as though it were a Buddhist scripture (that is, when circulating a conflated edition
one must clearly mark it as a conflated edition
), and moreover that conflating is difficult and must be undertaken by someone capable of it. From this one can
clearly see
Master Yinguang held that the Amitāyus Sutra can be conflated.
In fact, Master Lianchi said of the conflated edition:
“It has rendered great service to the Pure Land.”
Master Ouyi said of the conflated edition:
“This is indeed the wheel of Dharmākara's vows.”

In his celebrated work the Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra, whenever Master Lianchi cites the Amitāyus Sutra, he mostly quotes the Wang Conflated Edition, and only occasionally the original translations.
Master Youxi, in his celebrated work the Concise Exposition of the Amitābha Sutra with the Sub-commentary of the Perfect Middle, throughout quotes the Wang Conflated Edition.

Furthermore, Wang Longshu's conflated edition, having been examined and approved by eminent monks, was included in the Qianlong edition of the Canon. All of this shows that the eminent monks unanimously held that the Amitāyus Sutra can be conflated — as the saying goes, great minds think alike. How could Master Yinguang have stood outside this consensus? To say that Master Yinguang opposed the conflating of the Amitāyus Sutra is truly to wrong him.
